intro.text: Apps work much like websites underneath. Every time you open an app or tap something in it, the app sends a request to its own servers, and each request goes to a specific web address. Two layers of that traffic tell us what is happening.

subs.title: The two base-tier reports that matter most, explained

paragraphs.text: Content Usage (weekly and monthly). For every episode, and separately for every subscription plan, four numbers: Total Customers Streamed (unique people who played it), Total Number of Streams (play sessions: a valid stream is anything over 0 seconds through the Prime interface, and pressing play again or switching device starts a new one), Total Minutes Streamed (non-ad minutes) and Total Ad Minutes Streamed. So "how many people, how many times, how many minutes" per episode. There is no completion rate; minutes divided by customers against runtime is the proxy. Because the stream threshold is 0 seconds, stream counts run well above any viewer definition Crosswalk uses.

paragraphs.text: • Amazon reports only to its contracting partner. The Channels reports go to the channel operator (Peacock). paragraphs.text: What moves a seat's line: • Habits set the start. A seat starts higher when it is loyal to the show or 45 and older. A phone in hand while watching starts it lower. • Most of each move is the person's own reaction. About 70% is how they feel about the scene, and the rest is the pull of their habits. • The type of scene matters. Tender scenes lift seats that are women, LGBTQ+ or 45 and older. Funny scenes lift seats under 40. Action lifts men under 40. • Stage pushes the whole line. In the habit lifts every scene, and drifting away pulls every scene down. • Habits tilt big and quiet moments. A loyal seat gets more from a big moment, and a phone in hand drags talky stretches and silences. • Each line remembers. Every reading keeps most of the one before, so moves come in steps of a few points, and a real turn moves more. • A seat knows which cast member it sees. Time on screen alone never lifts a seat. • Reactions come only when something lands, at most two in any five scenes.
